caseStudies.title: Reconciliation AI
caseStudies.summary: An AI tool that matches ERP, bank and tax records, sends only the unclear items to a person, and logs every decision.

image.alt: Illustration of a rising financial chart over an office (not a product screenshot)

caseStudies.headline: Reconciliation AI: month-end close without the spreadsheet marathon
caseStudies.lede: We built an AI matching tool that ties every sale to its payment and its tax receipt. It shows where the gap comes from and puts each decision on record.
caseStudies.service: AI Workflow Automation · Custom Software & Integrations
overview: The client is a distribution business that sells across several depots. Customers pay by bank transfer, mobile money and cash. The finance team closes the books every month in their ERP, and every sale has to match a government tax receipt.

challenge.text: The ERP, the bank statements and the tax records each told part of the story. Nothing linked them.

challenge.lead: A gap nobody could explain fast.
challenge.text: Sales at the till didn't match what reached the ERP. Finding out why meant going row by row.
Bank charges, split payments and customer names spelled five different ways broke simple matching rules.
Credit notes and write-offs needed a named approver and a record no one could edit later.
One open item could hold up every task after it.

solution.text: We built a reconciliation workbench. The machine does the matching. People make the calls.

solution.lead: The AI never closes an item on its own.
solution.text: Each proposed match gets a confidence score and lands in one of three bands: certain, probable or needs review. The team can approve the certain band in one go. Anything less goes to a review lane, with an evidence panel that shows which records matched and why.

solution.lead: The confidence comes from the evidence, not from the model.
solution.text: A match scores high only when the supporting records actually line up. If the tool can't prove part of the gap, it says so. It does not guess.

solution.lead: It starts with the size of the problem.
solution.text: The tool takes the total unexplained gap and breaks it into causes: missing imports, sales with no tax receipt, unusual credit notes, high refunds. Finance can see where the money went before opening a single row.

solution.lead: Every action goes into a hash-chained audit log.
solution.text: Each entry links to the one before it. Change one entry and every entry after it breaks, so tampering shows.

features.text: Three-way matching across ERP entries, bank and mobile-money feeds, and tax receipts.
Confidence bands (certain, probable, review), with bulk approval for the certain band.
Fuzzy name matching that handles spelling differences, bank charges and split payments.
Evidence panel on every match, so reviewers see the reason, not just a score.
Gap breakdown chart showing how much of the gap each cause explains.
Anomaly flags for odd credit notes, missing receipts and high refund rates.
Write-offs above a set amount need a second approver.
Month-end close tracker that shows which tasks each open item is blocking.
Tamper-evident audit log you can replay. It records who did what, and when.

delivery.lead: Started from the client's own figures.
delivery.text: We worked from their real period data, not sample data, so the tool showed their actual problem from day one.
Confidence bands, tolerances and approval limits were agreed with the people who sign off the books.
Gap, match, exception, approval, close and audit, all in one web app.

cta.heading: Is your month-end close still a matching exercise?
cta.body: Send us one month of exports. We'll show you what matches, what doesn't, and why.

caseStudies.headline: CloudOps Console: a platform you can explain to your board and run at 3 a.m.
caseStudies.lede: We built the operations console behind a distribution platform. It covers releases, monitoring, incidents, security and data residency in one place.
caseStudies.service: Custom Software & Integrations · Cloud architecture, DevOps & SRE
overview: The client runs orders, dispatch and deliveries across several depots and a truck fleet. Their platform talks to an ERP, banks, mobile money, a tax authority, GPS trackers and weighbridges at the depot gates. Some of their data must, by law, stay in the country.

challenge.text: Leadership was asking simple questions with no clear answers. How is it built? Where is it hosted? Who can see what? Where does the data actually sit?
ERP calls time out. Bank APIs go down for maintenance. Payment providers send the same callback twice. Depot gates lose signal.
One bad release could stop orders across every depot.
Tax and customer records had to stay in the country, with a clear record of where everything else went.

solution.text: We built a single console for the people who run the platform, plus the architecture behind it.

solution.lead: Our rule: an outage can delay a message, never lose it.
solution.text: Every incoming order, payment and GPS ping is written to a durable event log before anything else happens. If the ERP is down, orders queue in their original order and post when it comes back. Finance sees a queue length, not missing data.

solution.lead: Releases go out in small steps.
solution.text: Each release goes to a small share of traffic first. If errors pass a set limit, it rolls back on its own. Production needs a named approval, and every approval is logged.

solution.lead: Every part of the system is documented the same way.
solution.text: What it runs on, how it scales, how it fails, and what still works when it's down. The client's IT team gets real sample payloads for each integration, ready to hand to their ERP, bank and tax contacts.

solution.lead: AI is one step in the pipeline, not a black box.
solution.text: Wherever AI reads documents or orders, it gives a confidence score. A person checks anything below the bar.

features.text: Lint, type checks, tests, a software bill of materials and a vulnerability scan that blocks high and critical issues. Images are signed.
Production approval gate with a named approver and an audit record.
Staged (canary) rollouts with automatic error-rate guardrails and one-click rollback. Rollbacks need a second approver.
Monitoring and alerts with service-level objectives and error budgets.
Incident response from first alert to mitigation to a blameless postmortem, all on one timeline.
Service map with regions, replicas and replication lag.
Reference architecture and integration contracts with real payload examples.
Role-based access by role and depot. If the depot context is missing, the system shows nothing rather than the wrong data.
Data residency map showing where each class of data lives, and what never leaves the country.
Hash-chained audit trail for every ingest, change and action, with safe replay that never touches live data.
Cloud cost view with spend by service and savings suggestions.

delivery.text: For each external system we wrote down how it fails and what the platform does when it does.

delivery.lead: Designed for the worst place first.
delivery.text: The depot gate has the weakest signal, so gate hardware buffers locally and syncs when the link returns.

delivery.lead: Wrote the security and residency model.
delivery.text: Encryption, access, key storage and data location were set per data class, not per service.
Built the console on top, so operators, IT and leadership all look at the same picture.

overview: JMarkets is an online broker. Its customers trade CFDs on currencies, indices and commodities. It serves Japanese-speaking traders.

challenge.text: Trading platforms are a target for scams. A new broker has to look credible from the first screen.
Many visitors don't know what a spread is, or how margin works. Without plain explanations, they leave.
Account opening, trading access, marketing campaigns and support often live in different systems. That adds friction for traders and staff.
A translated English site doesn't work. Layout, tone and content need to match how Japanese traders read and decide.

solution.text: We built a platform that takes a trader from “what is a CFD?” to their first trade, in Japanese, without sending them anywhere else.

solution.lead: A short path to the first trade.
solution.text: Account opening is three clear steps: create an account, verify identity (KYC), then fund and trade on MT4 or MT5. Each step says what happens next.

solution.lead: Education sits next to the trade.
solution.text: Short, plain answers explain CFDs, spreads and margin risk, with a nudge to try the demo first. Traders learn before they put money in.

solution.lead: Market context in one place.
solution.text: An economic calendar, market news, analysis and a glossary help traders understand why prices moved.

solution.lead: Risk is visible, not hidden.
solution.text: Risk disclosures and scam warnings appear across the site, not buried in the footer.

solution.lead: The business side is built in.
solution.text: Staff run campaigns and promotions and handle client support from the same platform.

features.text: Japanese-first design and copy across the whole platform.
Three-step account opening with identity verification (KYC).
MT4 / MT5 access on desktop (Windows, Mac) and mobile (iOS, Android).
Beginner Q&A on CFDs, spreads and margin, plus a route to the demo.
Market information hub: economic calendar, news, analysis and a glossary.
Campaign and promotion management for the marketing team.
Client support: FAQ, login help and support tools.
Risk disclosures and fraud warnings on every page.

delivery.text: Mapped the trader journey from first visit to first trade, and cut every step that wasn't needed.
Short answers up front, with detail one click away.
Built the site and staff tools on one platform, so campaigns and support don't need separate systems.

Japanese companies want a creative partner at home. Overseas companies want help selling in Japan. Each needs to find its own path.
The studio splits work between people and AI on purpose. People handle ideas and direction. AI handles repetitive production. That had to be explained simply, without sounding like a gimmick.

blogPosts.title: The Hidden Cost of Manual Workflows: Why Automation ROI Is Always Higher Than You Think
blogPosts.excerpt: Most businesses underestimate how much manual work costs them. We break down the real numbers and show why automation ROI compounds over time.
blogPosts.question: What does manual work really cost you?
blogPosts.quote: A business running on automation can 10x volume without 10x headcount.
blogPosts.body:
Every business has manual workflows. The question is: do you know how much they really cost you?

The obvious costs are easy to calculate: the salary of the person doing the work. But the hidden costs are far larger. The errors they make, and the time spent fixing them. The delays caused by waiting for human input. The opportunities missed because the process was too slow. And the mental overhead of managing it all.

A mid sized e-commerce business processing 200 orders per day, with manual data entry between its store, warehouse and accounting system, typically loses 3 to 4 hours of staff time per day to pure data transfer. At ₹500 an hour, that's ₹5,000 to ₹6,000 a day, or about ₹15 to 18 lakhs per year. Add another 20 to 30% for error costs such as wrong orders and reconciliation issues.

Automation ROI compounds. Not just because it eliminates the ongoing cost, but because it enables scale. A business that runs on manual workflows can't grow beyond what its team can manually process. A business running on automation can 10x volume without 10x headcount.

At WeSee, we've run detailed automation ROI analyses for dozens of clients. In every case, the return on a well designed automation exceeds the cost within 90 days. Often within 45.

blogPosts.title: Building Your First AI Chatbot: A Guide for Indian SMEs
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical guide in plain language to building and deploying your first AI chatbot, tailored for Indian small and medium businesses.
blogPosts.question: Where should your first chatbot start?
blogPosts.quote: You don't need to train your own AI. You need to configure and deploy one.
blogPosts.body:
If you run a small or medium business in India and you're thinking about building an AI chatbot, this guide is for you. Not the theoretical version. The practical one.

First, the good news: building an AI chatbot for your business has never been more accessible. The underlying technology (large language models) is now available as APIs, and the cost of running them is low enough for businesses of any size. You don't need to train your own AI. You need to configure and deploy one.

Step one is always defining the job. What do you want the chatbot to do? Answer FAQs about your products? Qualify leads? Book appointments? Take orders on WhatsApp? The clearer you are about the specific job, the better your chatbot will perform.

Step two is choosing your deployment channel. In India, WhatsApp is almost always the answer: more than 500 million users, a familiar interface, and no app download required. For higher ticket or B2B businesses, a website chat widget works well alongside WhatsApp.

Step three is connecting the AI to your knowledge base: your product catalogue, FAQs, pricing, policies and processes. This is what turns a generic chatbot into one that actually knows about your business.

WeSee has built AI chatbots for clients ranging from local businesses with 10 people to enterprises worth 200 crore. The process is the same. What changes is the complexity of the knowledge base and the integrations required.
